H5b5bde33ed980a76.similarities: Both cases involve a mortgagor granting a lease during mortgage pendency, with subsequent disputes over whether the lease binds the mortgagee after redemption or enforcement.
H5b5bde33ed980a76.differences: The current case concerns a permanent lease under pre-1929 law where security sufficiency was the test, while the historical case involves statutory occupancy rights arising from a mortgagee settlement, not a mortgagor's lease.
H5b5bde33ed980a76.warrant: The historical case clarifies that mortgagee settlements creating occupancy rights differ from mortgagor leases, which are governed by security sufficiency tests under the Transfer of Property Act.

actors.reason: Current case involves mortgagor-lessee; historical case involves mortgagee-settlor-tenant.

property.reason: Both involve mortgaged land subject to lease/settlement disputes.

time.reason: Current case is pre-1929; historical case involves post-settlement occupancy rights.

procedure.reason: Both involve appellate review of lower court possession decrees.

request.reason: Current case seeks lease invalidity; historical case seeks possession against occupancy rights.

H5b5bde33ed980a76.limited_use: The historical case distinguishes mortgagee settlements from mortgagor leases, limiting its direct application to the current lease validity question.
H5b5bde33ed980a76.limitations: The historical case addresses statutory occupancy rights, which do not apply to the pre-1929 lease validity test based on security sufficiency.

SRca31e0195692e970.content: Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950 arises from a judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Patna dated 26th January, 1944, which itself stemmed from a decree of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh in Title Suit No. 45 of 1939.
SRca31e0195692e970.speaker: CIVIL APPELLATE, JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950

record_scope.event: Case jurisdiction and procedural history defined

SR6105d83870a1e737.content: The central legal question is whether, prior to the 1929 enactment of Section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act, a mortgagor in possession had the power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee.
SR6105d83870a1e737.speaker: BHAGWATI J

SRc861336bccd1163c.content: Raja Nilkanth Narain Singh mortgaged Gadi Sirampur to the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited on 1st August, 1914. The Bank obtained a mortgage decree on 29th November, 1921, and purchased a third share on 28th October, 1922.
SRc861336bccd1163c.speaker: Narrative of Facts

SRa7796579ce36c970.content: During the pendency of mortgage proceedings, on 5th November, 1925, Wazir Narain Singh granted a permanent lease of four villages to Hiraman Ram, Manager and Karta of his joint Hindu family, and his son Chohan Ram.
SRa7796579ce36c970.speaker: Narrative of Facts

record_scope.event: Permanent lease granted during mortgage suit pendency
record_scope.procedure: Court of Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh

SRb8df43a03806601b.content: An agreement was made that if Wazir Narain Singh paid Rs. 1,10,631-4-0 by 16th August, 1926, the sale would be set aside. He executed a mortgage on 14th August, 1926, to the Court of Wards to satisfy dues and set aside the sale.
SRb8df43a03806601b.speaker: Narrative of Facts

record_scope.event: Sale set aside and new mortgage executed

SRe56553556cf6a879.content: The Plaintiff (through the Manager of the Court of Wards) filed a suit on 4th February, 1929, to enforce the mortgage, impleading Hiraman Ram and Dilo Ram as co-defendants. A final decree for sale was passed on 18th September, 1931.
SRe56553556cf6a879.speaker: Narrative of Facts

SR49a85ac37c355063.content: Dilo Ram died after the mortgage decree. Hiraman Ram and his son Chohan Ram continued in actual possession. The Plaintiff filed the suit on 16th November, 1939, against them for khas possession of the villages.
SR49a85ac37c355063.speaker: Narrative of Facts

record_scope.procedure: Court of Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh

SR43b1f9b4f4974e70.content: Defendant 2 contended that the Plaintiff was not subrogated to the Bank's position, the decree was not binding as he was not a party, the Patta was not ended by the auction sale, and a partition occurred within a year allotting properties to him.
SR43b1f9b4f4974e70.speaker: Defendant 2

HA64fcfcafce14c6f9.content: Plaintiffs redeemed mortgage in June 1942 but were resisted by Gopes (Defendant 1) upon taking possession, leading to this suit after failed criminal proceedings.
HA64fcfcafce14c6f9.speaker: The mortgage was redeemed in June 1942 by payment in proceedings under section 83 of the Transfer of Property Act, When the plaintiffs went to take possession, they were resisted by the Gopes (defendant first party), and after unsuccessful criminal proceedings, the plaintiffs filed the present suit.

HAe881a4371c2e77a1.content: Subordinate Judge dismissed suit holding Gopes were raiyats with permanent occupancy rights from settlement by mortgagee Lakhandeo Singh.
HAe881a4371c2e77a1.speaker: The Subordinate Judge dismissed it, holding that the Gopes were raiyats having acquired permanent occupancy rights in the lands as the result of the settlement by the mortgagee, Lakhandeo Singh.

HAeca00ceb9e908a7c.content: High Court set aside Subordinate Judge's decision, granting plaintiffs possession decree finding defendants were not raiyats with no permanent occupancy rights.
HAeca00ceb9e908a7c.speaker: On appeal the High Court set aside this decision and gave the plaintiffs a decree for possession on the finding that the defendants were not raiyats and had no permanent rights of occupancy.

HA6e642f3ce8568cbb.content: Plaintiffs alleged lands were their zirat lands under Bihar Tenancy Act section 116, preventing defendants from acquiring occupancy rights.
HA6e642f3ce8568cbb.speaker: At the trial, the plaintiffs alleged and maintained that the lands were their zirat lands within the meaning of section 116 of the Bihar Tenancy Act and that the defendant first party could acquire no rights of occupancy in the same.

HA343dfedabf3f510a.content: Subordinate Judge found against plaintiffs, holding lands were khud kasht or bakasht proprietor lands where occupancy rights can be acquired.
HA343dfedabf3f510a.speaker: The Subordinate Judge found against this contention and held that they were khud kasht or bakasht lands of the proprietor, in which rights of occupancy can be acquired.

HA05a22282ed390fd1.content: Privy Council in Bengal Indigo Company v. Roghobur Das held zuripeshgi lease is security for money advanced, not mere cultivation contract.
HA05a22282ed390fd1.speaker: It was held by the Privy Council in Bengal Indigo Company v. Roghobur Das that a zuripeshgi lease is not a mere contract for the cultivation of the land at a rent, but is a security to the tenant for the money advanced.

H705caa40b1cc6090.similarities: Both cases involve courts analyzing conflicting documentary evidence to determine if parties acted as a joint family or separate entities, relying on business conduct and deed descriptions to infer legal relationships.
H705caa40b1cc6090.differences: The current case focuses on the statutory power of a mortgagor to lease property before 1929, whereas the historical case concerns the factual determination of joint family status from ambiguous documents; the current case applies Transfer of Property Act rules while the historical case applies Hindu law principles of separation.
H705caa40b1cc6090.warrant: The historical analysis of conflicting deeds and conduct regarding family status provides an analogical framework for assessing the weight of documentary evidence in the current case, though the legal standards for binding leases differ.

actors.reason: Current case involves mortgagor/mortgagee/lessee; historical case involves brothers/uncle/nephew.

property.reason: Current case involves mortgaged villages; historical case involves disputed ancestral property.

time.reason: Current case spans 1914-1952; historical case spans 1898-1922.

procedure.reason: Both involve appellate review of lower court findings on factual/legal disputes.

request.reason: Current case seeks possession based on lease invalidity; historical case seeks title determination.

H705caa40b1cc6090.limited_use: The historical case illustrates how courts weigh conflicting documentary evidence to determine legal status, but it does not establish the statutory rules governing mortgagor leasing powers.
H705caa40b1cc6090.limitations: The historical case addresses factual joint family status under Hindu law, whereas the current case requires application of the Transfer of Property Act regarding lease validity and mortgage security.

HA795497fa66e5b94d.content: The court rejects the appellants' claim that a 1898 document proves Ram Narain and Ram Saran were joint owners, noting the property locations and areas differ from earlier joint records.
HA795497fa66e5b94d.speaker: Reporting Court

HA2987c3d0f73d5d58.content: Documents from 1905 show Ram Narain and Ram Saran conducting joint business for 20 years, leading the High Court to infer they likely became a flourishing joint concern.
HA2987c3d0f73d5d58.speaker: Reporting Court

HAa8db70c1c1c44fd5.content: The court questions whether later documents showing joint conduct can destroy the inference of separation drawn from earlier documents, noting they lived like a joint family due to kinship.
HAa8db70c1c1c44fd5.speaker: Reporting Court

HA0447c0a42c63443a.content: The court holds that a statement in a lease deed describing Ram Narain and Ram Saran as joint does not contradict an earlier mortgage stating all three brothers were separated.
HA0447c0a42c63443a.speaker: Reporting Court

HA8ce4ed88c18c9b7b.content: The court notes a sale deed by a stranger vendor recited the purchasers were uncle and nephew forming a joint family, which is described as somewhat surprising.
HA8ce4ed88c18c9b7b.speaker: Reporting Court

HA77fca7d642633eab.content: The court concludes that a proper consideration of all sale deeds does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that there was no original separation between the parties.
HA77fca7d642633eab.speaker: Reporting Court
